sections.overview: The Purple Emperor is a large European and Asian woodland butterfly, most often encountered high in the tree canopy. Its caterpillars depend on willows growing in sunny clearings and shaded woodland edges.
sections.identification: Both sexes have dark brown wings with a broad white band and orange-ringed eyespots; the male flashes iridescent blue-purple in oblique light, while the female is larger-looking and lacks that sheen. Published wingspans vary by region and guide, roughly 55–92 mm, with no consistent sex-specific measurement in the sources reviewed.
sections.habitat: It uses broadleaved, mixed and sometimes coniferous forests, especially edges, rides and clearings with semi-shaded willows. The species ranges widely across Europe and temperate Asia, but local populations can be sparse and difficult to observe.
sections.diet: Caterpillars feed mainly on goat willow (Salix caprea) and grey willow (S. cinerea), with other willows used in some regions. Adults rarely visit flowers: they take tree sap and aphid honeydew, and descend to damp ground, dung or carrion for salts and minerals.
sections.behavior: Adults spend much of the day in the canopy, and males often descend to feed at damp patches or animal droppings. Males defend high perches and may gather around especially tall trees where they wait for passing females.
sections.reproduction: Females lay single eggs on willow leaves in summer, and the species normally produces one generation each year. The green caterpillar bears two short horn-like projections on its head and overwinters attached near a willow bud before feeding again in spring.
sections.ecology: Its close relative the Lesser Purple Emperor (Apatura ilia) can also show iridescent color, so do not identify this species from sheen alone. Compare the full underside pattern and the orange markings; the two species also differ in the willow and poplar hosts used by their caterpillars.
sections.conservation: A French national assessment published in 2012 classed the species as Least Concern, while a 2026 regional assessment lists it as Near Threatened in Burgundy–Franche-Comté. These categories apply at different geographic scales and dates, not to every local population equally.
